question:
Patient note:
A 51-year-old man is reviewed in the pre-operative holding area this afternoon ahead of a planned right shoulder arthroscopy for debridement of a degenerative rotator-cuff tear; the orthopedic consultant anticipates less than an hour of scope time under general anesthesia with same-day discharge if post-anesthetic recovery is smooth. Four weeks ago the patient slipped on wet decking and sustained a nondisplaced mid-shaft humeral bruise that was managed non-operatively, but at the same visit radiographs of the right ankle revealed no fracture even though soft-tissue swelling required an above-ankle fiberglass cast to control pain and protect the lateral collateral ligaments. That cast was applied twenty-six days ago and remains in situ today, extending to just below the knee with a window cut over the malleolus for neurovascular checks; physical therapy notes document that since application he has been allowed only brief transfers from bed to chair and has otherwise spent the majority of each day supine with the leg elevated on pillows. He has not visited an operating room, endoscopy suite, or interventional radiology bay in the interim, and there have been no systemic infections, heart-failure exacerbations, or respiratory tract pneumonias requiring antimicrobial therapy during that convalescence. Past medical history is notable for moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributed to a 25-pack-year cigarette exposure; he quit eight years ago but still uses a combination short-acting beta-agonist and ipratropium inhaler two or three times a week, and pulmonary clinic spirometry six months earlier showed an FEV1 at 65 % of predicted without significant reversibility. He denies chronic oxygen use, recent exacerbations, or steroid bursts over the last year. Five years ago, during a hematology consultation for pre-operative screening before elective knee arthroscopy, he was found to carry a heterozygous prothrombin G20210A mutation; simultaneous testing for factor V Leiden returned negative, and no other thrombophilic markers were detected. Despite that genetic finding he has never experienced calf pain, unilateral swelling, pleuritic chest discomfort, or radiologically confirmed venous or pulmonary clot, and none of his first-degree relatives have required anticoagulation for unexplained thrombosis. He reports no malignancies current or remote, no inflammatory bowel disease, and no endocrine or rheumatologic disorders. Medications this morning include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled once daily, as-needed albuterol-ipratropium combination, and over-the-counter acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours for shoulder aching; he takes no hormone therapy, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, or antiplatelet drugs. On arrival he is fasting since midnight, has voided recently, and removed all jewelry. Vital signs taken ten minutes ago record temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, heart rate 76 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, respirations 16 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air. Airway evaluation reveals Mallampati class II with full cervical range and intact dentition. Jugular venous pulse lies below the clavicle, carotid upstrokes are brisk, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and there is no peripheral edema. Auscultation of the lungs demonstrates scattered expiratory wheezes at both bases that clear after coached deep breathing; no crackles are appreciated. Abdominal examination is benign. Inspection of the lower extremities shows a well-padded fiberglass cast on the right leg with intact skin margins, toes warm and pink, capillary refill less than two seconds, and posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses 2+ via Doppler; the contralateral calf is supple without varicosities, tenderness, or pitting, and circumferences measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosities are 38 cm bilaterally. There is no upper-extremity central venous catheter, implantable port, or peripherally inserted central line; intravenous access today consists of a single 20-gauge cannula in the left cephalic vein running lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate. Neurologic screen is normal, and the operative shoulder displays pain-limited abduction above 90° but preserves 5/5 strength in elbow flexion and grip. Laboratory studies drawn at 06:00 reveal hemoglobin 14.1 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 42 %, leukocytes 7.2 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, platelets 248 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 139 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.0 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.89 mg dL⁻¹, AST 22 U L⁻¹, ALT 24 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.6 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. An electrocardiogram reviewed by anesthesia shows normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats min⁻¹, normal intervals, and no ischemic changes; upright portable chest radiography obtained yesterday demonstrates hyperinflated lung fields characteristic of his underlying airway disease but no infiltrate, consolidation, or pleural effusion. Body-mass index is calculated at 24 kg m⁻². Pneumatic calf compression sleeves are already fitted to both lower limbs but remain uninflated until induction, and no chemoprophylactic anticoagulant has yet been administered while surgical and anesthesia teams finalize the intra-operative plan.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
Caprini surgical VTE risk score (2013 model). The operative-duration category is uncertain: “less than an hour” does not specify whether anesthesia plus surgery will exceed 45 minutes. Assuming the planned outpatient procedure qualifies as minor surgery:
- Age 51 (41–60 years) → 1.
- COPD with abnormal spirometry → 1.
- Planned minor surgery → 1.
- Immobilizing lower-leg cast applied within the past month → 2.
- Bed confinement for more than 72 hours, with transfers only → 2.
- Known prothrombin G20210A thrombophilia → 3.
No additional factor is documented; the ankle injury was not a fracture. Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10. If operative and anesthesia time exceeds 45 minutes, the procedure contributes 2 instead of 1.
Final answer: 10
